name: Jätte
description: Jättar (giants) are colossal humanoid beings from Swedish folklore, believed to be an ancient race that lived in the land long before humans. The word "jätte" derives from an Old Germanic verb meaning "to eat," reflecting their immense appetites. In Swedish folk tradition, jättar are most famously associated with features of the landscape: glacial erratic boulders called jättekast (giant's throws) were said to have been hurled by angry giants attempting to crush churches, whose bells they could not stand. Mountain formations resembling footprints or cooking cauldrons were also attributed to giants. According to widespread belief, most jättar fled the land when Christianity arrived, but some remained in remote mountains and forests into comparatively modern times. Unlike the wise and ancient jötnar of Norse mythology, later Swedish folklore giants are often portrayed as strong but dim-witted, easily outsmarted by clever humans. Famous Swedish giant tales include "Pojken som åt i kapp med jätten" (The Boy Who Ate Race with the Giant) and the story of Jätten Finn who built Lund Cathedral
source: Swedish folklore

name: Jörmungandr (Faroese)
description: In Faroese folklore, the Norse World Serpent Jörmungandr appears in a unique creation myth explaining the origin of the archipelago. After the World Serpent (child of Loki) was defeated in the final battles of the gods, a tooth fell from the dying serpent's enormous mouth into the ocean and became the Faroe Islands. This dramatic origin story connects Faroese identity directly to the great Norse mythological cycle, positioning the islands as a fragment of a cosmic being. An alternative folk explanation claims the islands were formed from dirt that gathered under God's fingernails while He created the world and was flicked away. Both accounts were preserved through Faroese oral tradition and recorded in ballad form. The Jörmungandr version is the more dramatic and poetic of the two, reflecting the deep Norse heritage of the Faroese people who preserved the Old Norse language and mythology in their kvæði (ballads) long after other Scandinavian cultures had Christianized
source: Norse mythology; the Midgard Serpent that encircles the world.

name: Juan Bobo (Puerto Rican Trickster Folk Hero)
description: Juan Bobo (Simple John) is the beloved trickster folk hero of Puerto Rican folklore -- a simple-minded but well-intentioned young boy whose absurd misunderstandings and literal interpretations of his mother instructions create a cascade of hilarious disasters. For over 200 years, Juan Bobo stories have been a cornerstone of Puerto Rican oral tradition and children literature. He is simultaneously a fool and a trickster: his actions are driven by genuine kindness and good intentions, but his complete lack of common sense leads to catastrophes. In the most famous tale, his mother tells him to care for the family pig while she attends church. When the pig squeals, Juan assumes it wants to go to mass too, so he dresses it in his mother finest Sunday dress, puts lipstick and jewelry on it, and sends it to church -- with predictably disastrous results. Juan Bobo stories originated from Spanish picaresque traditions (influenced by Lazarillo de Tormes and Don Quixote) and evolved through centuries of Puerto Rican oral tradition
source: Puerto Rican oral tradition, Puerto Rico folklore

name: Juoksáhkká
description: Juoksáhkká (Bow Woman) is a Sami goddess depicted with a bow on Sami shaman drums. She is one of the three daughters of Máttaráhkká, the origin mother. Her most distinctive power is the ability to change a child's sex from female to male in the womb if given sufficient offerings — an important ability in a culture where sons were valued for hunting. She helps with fetal development and birth, protects children from gunshots and falls, and helps women during menstruation. After a son was born, a small bow and arrow symbol was placed in Sáráhkká's porridge and then placed beside the cradle so the boy would grow into a skilled archer. Her name connects her to the god of hunting Lieaibolmmái (the Alder Man), to whose protection she entrusted baby boys after birth. Like her sisters, she was known only among Scandinavian Sami (Norway and Sweden)
source: Wikipedia (Juoksáhkká); baalka.se; Ganander 1789

name: Juovlastállu
description: Juovlastállu (Yule Stállu) is the terrifying Christmas giant of Sami folklore, a variant of Stállo who punishes children who misbehave at Christmastime. Unlike the regular Stállo who is primarily a cannibal, Juovlastállu functions as a disciplinary figure — he enforces proper Christmas behavior. He drives a sled (ráidu) pulled by mice or lemmings through the winter landscape. Families must sweep the area around their home clean so the sled doesn't get stuck on woodchips or debris. Water must be left outside for him; if denied water, he becomes enraged and may suck blood from humans. He whistles sharply in the wind and the sound of his pipe can be dangerous to hearing. He is invisible yet everywhere during the Christmas season. He can assume the shape of the moon and enter the tent through the smoke vent in the roof. He demands that people stay inside and remain quiet during Christmas. If children are noisy or naughty, he stuffs them in his sack and abducts them, either eating them or returning them much later. He lives in a large gorge. The tradition connects to the Norse Wild Hunt (Oskoreia/Juleskreia) and the Setesdal tradition of Ståle's journey
source: Qvigstad recordings; skolerom.no; SNL.no; levandekulturarv.se

name: Jutulkloa
description: Jutulkloa (the Giant's Claw) is a legendary giant associated with a distinctive rock formation on the Fosen coast of Trøndelag. The name combines 'jutul' (a regional variant of jøtul, meaning giant) and 'klo' (claw). According to legend, a jutul who lived in the Fosen mountains reached out his hand to grab a passing ship, but the sun rose and turned him to stone, leaving only his enormous claw-like fingers visible as rock formations along the coast. The jutul was known for terrorizing coastal communities by overturning boats and stealing cattle. Different versions of the legend are told in fishing communities along the Fosen coastline, with varying explanations for the rock formation — some say it is the claw of a sea giant who attacked ships, others say it is the hand of a mountain giant who reached for the sea. The legend is part of a broader Norwegian tradition of giants being turned to stone by sunlight
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Kaliya (Multi-Headed Serpent)
description: Kaliya is a massive multi-headed serpent (naga) who lived in the Yamuna River during Lord Krishna's childhood in Vrindavan. According to the Bhagavata Purana, Kaliya had fled to the Yamuna from the ocean out of fear of his enemy, Garuda (the eagle deity). The serpent's presence poisoned the river — the water boiled with venom, killing fish, birds, and trees along the banks. The land for half a kos around the river became barren, and the villagers could no longer approach the water. Young Krishna, barely a child, dove into the deepest part of the river to confront the serpent. Kaliya wrapped Krishna in his coils, but Krishna expanded his body, broke free, and began dancing on Kaliya's thousand hoods. As Krishna danced, each hood was crushed under his divine feet until the serpent, bleeding and exhausted, surrendered. Kaliya's wives prayed to Krishna for mercy. Spared but banished, Kaliya and his family were sent to the ocean, and the Yamuna was restored to purity
source: Bhagavata Purana, Harivamsa, Krishna folklore

name: Kan'du Fureytha (Ocean Demon of Fuvahmulah)
description: Kan'du Fureytha (Ocean Demon) is a malevolent sea spirit from the folklore of Fuvahmulah, the southernmost atoll of the Maldives. According to local legend, this demon emerged from the ocean as a 'pale, large flame looming over the rocks,' terrifying the islanders of Fuvahmulah. It would drag people into the sea, drowning them, and was blamed for numerous disappearances of fishermen and swimmers. The terrified islanders sought help from Edhurutakkaange Mohamed Didi, a renowned fanditha veriyaa (sorcerer) of exceptional power. Despite working his magic for many days at the reef where the demon was most active, the Kan'du Fureytha kept claiming victims. Tormented by his failed attempts, Mohamed Didi cast one ultimate, all-powerful spell that trapped the demon forever within a deserted island. Shortly afterward, the island mysteriously vanished entirely beneath the waves, never to be seen again. A large reef rock called Fureytha Gaa ('Demon Rock') now marks the spot where the island once stood. Local tradition holds that if you prod the stone with an iron rod, it still oozes blood, and will continue to do so forever whenever struck
source: Maldivian oral tradition, Xavier Romero-Frias 'Folk Tales of the Maldives'

name: Karkadann
description: The Karkadann is a legendary beast from Persian and Arabic mythology, often described as the Persian version of the unicorn. This powerful creature was believed to inhabit the grassy plains of India, Persia, and North Africa, and is based on the Indian rhinoceros as described by early scholars. First documented in the 10th and 11th centuries by the Persian scholar Al-Biruni, the Karkadann evolved in later writings from a simple rhinoceros-like animal into a fearsome mythical beast endowed with magical properties. It appears in the famous collection One Thousand and One Nights during the Second Voyage of Sinbad the Sailor, where it is described as a ferocious beast that drives even elephants from its territory. The Karkadann horn is said to have powerful medicinal properties and can neutralize poisons
source: Persian mythology — the Karkadann unicorn-like beast documented in Persian bestiaries.

name: Kasa-obake
description: Kasa-obake, also known as karakasa-obake or karakasa-kozo, is a tsukumogami from Japanese folklore, a spirit that inhabits old, discarded umbrellas that have transformed into supernatural beings after many years of service. This yokai became particularly popular during the Edo period when artists like Toriyama Sekien included it in their illustrated collections of supernatural beings. Unlike many yokai that have extensive oral traditions, the kasa-obake is believed to have originated primarily through visual art and literature rather than traditional folk tales. It represents the Japanese animistic belief that even inanimate objects possess souls and can become animated, especially when treated with neglect or disrespect. The kasa-obake is one of the most recognizable and beloved of the tsukumogami yokai
source: Japanese folklore — Kasa-obake umbrella monster documented in Japanese yōkai tradition.

name: Kataragama Deviyo (Guardian of the Jungle)
description: Kataragama Deviyo is one of the four guardian deities of Sri Lanka and the patron deity of the Kataragama shrine, one of the island's most important multi-religious pilgrimage sites. He is identified with the Hindu god Murugan (Skanda/Kartikeya), the war god and son of Shiva, but in the Sinhalese Buddhist context, he is revered as a powerful guardian deity. According to legend, Kataragama traveled to Sri Lanka from India and fell in love with Valli, a Vedda (indigenous) tribal girl, at Kataragama in the southeastern jungle. Their marriage symbolizes the union between north Indian (Aryan) and indigenous Dravidian peoples. The Kataragama temple complex is unique in Sri Lanka as a site where Sinhalese Buddhists, Sri Lankan Tamils, Vedda people, and even Muslims worship together. He is associated with power, protection, and the fulfillment of vows. Devotees undertake extreme austerities at his shrine — fire-walking, kavadi (burden) dancing, and piercing their bodies with hooks and spears — as acts of devotion and thanksgiving. Kataragama Deviyo is also known as Mahasen Deviyo or Katharagama Deviyo in Sinhalese tradition
source: Sinhala Buddhist traditions, Kanda Puranam, Paul Wirz 'Kataragama', Sri Lankan pilgrimage traditions

name: Kaugjagjuk
description: Kaugjagjuk is a mischievous trickster figure from Inuit folklore, known for his clever pranks, shape-shifting abilities, and the valuable moral lessons embedded in his adventures. This small, agile spirit is a beloved character in Inuit oral tradition, where his stories are told to entertain and educate both children and adults. Like many trickster figures across world cultures, Kaugjagjuk uses wit and deception to outsmart larger and more powerful opponents, often exposing greed, arrogance, and foolishness in the process. His tales serve a dual purpose: providing entertainment during the long Arctic winters while teaching important lessons about proper behavior, sharing, humility, and respect for others. Kaugjagjuk represents the clever underdog who triumphs through intelligence rather than brute strength
source: Canada mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Keeper (Maya)
description: Keeper is a guardian spirit from Maya folklore as practiced in Mexico, particularly in the Yucatan Peninsula, Chiapas, and Quintana Roo regions where Maya traditions remain vibrant. These powerful beings are the custodians of sacred locations including cenotes, ancient pyramid complexes, underground rivers, and jungle-hidden ruins that dot the Mexican landscape. The Maya believe that every significant natural feature has a spiritual guardian assigned to protect it, maintaining the cosmic order established by the gods. Keepers serve as the bridge between the mundane world and the realm of the divine, ensuring that humans do not overstep their bounds or disrespect the sacred geography inherited from the ancestors. Their role is especially important at cenotes, which are considered portals to the underworld
source: Regional survey of Mesoamerican indigenous traditions — Maya, Aztec, Mixtec, Zapotec, and related peoples as documented in codices, ethnographies by Sahagún, Landa, and contemporary folklore collections.

name: Keiju
description: Keiju are ethereal fairy beings from Finnish folklore, known as tiny, beautiful humanoids with translucent wings resembling those of dragonflies or butterflies. These delicate spirits inhabit the liminal spaces of the Finnish wilderness, particularly forest ponds, misty meadows, and the edges of deep woodlands where sunlight filters through the canopy. Keiju are considered nature spirits closely connected to the vitality of the forest and its waterways, dancing among wildflowers and resting on water lilies when they are not visible to human eyes. Unlike the more dangerous spirits of Finnish mythology such as the Hiisi or the Näkki, Keiju are generally benevolent, though they are shy and prefer to avoid human contact. They are believed to emerge primarily during the brief Finnish summer when the midnight sun illuminates the landscape with perpetual twilight
source: Finnish mythology, Kalevala compiled by Elias Lönnrot

name: Kel Tamasheq Spirits (Tuareg Nature Spirits)
description: The Kel Tamasheq (People of the Tamasheq language) nature spirits are a diverse class of supernatural beings in Tuareg belief from the Sahara (Mali, Niger, Algeria, Libya). The most powerful are the Kel Essuf (the Wild Ones), spirits of the uninhabited desert. These beings are neither jinn nor angels but a distinct class of spirits unique to Tuareg cosmology. They inhabit remote plateaus (tassili), dry riverbeds, and solitary mountains. Some are benevolent and guide lost travelers; snip others harass camps and steal milk from goats. They are closely associated with the Tuareg alphabet (Tifinagh) and left inscriptions on rocks. The most dangerous are the Kel Tafukt (Spirits of the Sun), who cause heatstroke. Tuareg oral tradition says these spirits taught the ancestors the Tifinagh script and how to survive in the desert
source: Tuareg oral tradition, Saharan rock art traditions

name: Spirits of Kerkennah (Enchanted Island)
description: The Kerkennah Islands, a low-lying archipelago off the coast of Tunisia, are steeped in mystery and legend. According to local folklore, these islands were once part of a vast and wealthy kingdom that sank into the sea due to a divine curse—a legend reminiscent of the Atlantis myth. Today, the remaining islands are believed to be inhabited by spirits, the ghosts of the kingdom's former inhabitants. Fishermen and locals report strange phenomena: unexplained lights flickering over the water at night, sounds of phantom voices carried on the wind, and the sensation of being watched when alone on the beaches. The spirits are generally described as benign but melancholic, forever bound to the place where their kingdom fell. The Kerkennah Islands have a unique landscape of very low-lying land, extensive seagrass meadows, and ancient olive groves that can feel otherworldly. The legend adds to the islands' mysterious atmosphere and has become part of their cultural identity. Some versions of the myth suggest that the sunken kingdom can still be glimpsed on unusually calm days beneath the waves
source: Carthage Magazine; Tunisian oral traditions

name: Khas-uu
description: Khas-uu is a powerful tiger spirit from Mongolian folklore, deeply revered as the guardian spirit of the southern forest regions of Mongolia. Once roaming the forested slopes of the Khentii and Khangai mountain ranges, these magnificent spirits are now considered rare, with their numbers greatly diminished by hunting and habitat loss over the centuries. However, Mongolian traditions hold that the Khas-uu still prowls the remaining wilderness, watching over its territory with ancient wisdom and supernatural power. The tiger spirit is intimately associated with concepts of royalty, authority, and untamed natural power in Mongolian culture, serving as a symbol of the wild beauty that once dominated the southern landscape. It is considered both a physical animal and a spiritual entity that transcends the boundary between the natural and supernatural worlds
source: Mongolian folklore — Khas Uu animal spirit.

name: Khorba Spirits (Berber Ruin Dwellers)
description: Khorba spirits are supernatural beings in Berber folklore from Morocco and Algeria that inhabit abandoned buildings, ancient ruins, and collapsed granaries (the word 'khorba' means ruin or dilapidated building in Maghrebi Arabic and Berber dialects). These spirits are considered the guardians of forgotten places, protecting the remnants of previous civilizations. They are particularly associated with ksour (fortified villages) and granaries in the Atlas Mountains and the pre-Saharan valleys. Unlike the more generic jinn, Khorba spirits are tied to specific ruins and are believed to be the lingering spirits of the original inhabitants. They cause mischief: hiding tools, making noises at night, and leading people away from the ruins. However, they also protect the ruins from being completely destroyed or looted
source: Berber oral tradition, Maghrebi folklore

name: Khun Borom (Founder King of the Lao)
description: Khun Borom (Lao: ຂຸນບູລົມ) is the legendary founder-king of the Lao and Tai peoples, sent from heaven by the sky god Phaya Thaen to rule the earthly realm. According to the Nithan Khun Borom chronicle, after a great flood destroyed humanity, three righteous chiefs were preserved in heaven. They returned to earth with a sacred buffalo; when the buffalo died, a bitter gourd vine grew from its nostril, producing gourds from which the new human race emerged — darker-skinned peoples from gourds cut with a hot skewer, and lighter-skinned Tai peoples from gourds cut with a chisel. As the population grew, Phaya Thaen sent his own son Khun Borom to rule. He descended on a royal elephant with crossed tusks to Muang Then (modern Dien Bien Phu). After 25 years of rule, Khun Borom divided his kingdom among his seven sons, who became founders of the Tai kingdoms including Lan Xang (Laos), Lanna, Ayutthaya, and others. The legend establishes Khun Borom as the ancestor of all Tai-speaking peoples and the founder of Lao kingship
source: Lao chronicles (Nithan Khun Borom), Tai oral tradition

name: Kibanda
description: Kibanda is a water spirit from the folklore of the Bunyoro region of Uganda, deeply respected by local fishing communities who depend on the waters of Lake Bunyoro and its surrounding waterways for their livelihood. This powerful aquatic being is considered the master of the lakes fisheries, controlling the abundance or scarcity of fish based on its assessment of human behavior. Kibanda is known to manifest in multiple forms, most commonly described as either a gigantic python that coils beneath the waters surface or an enormous hippopotamus that rises from the depths. Fishermen approach the waters with great reverence, knowing that their catch depends entirely on the favor of this spirit. The Kibanda tradition reflects the deep connection between East African communities and their aquatic environments, where spiritual beliefs govern sustainable resource use and community ethics
source: Ugandan folklore — Kibanda water spirit documented in Ugandan oral tradition.

name: Kiev Ghost
description: The Kiev Ghost is a legendary phantom from Ukrainian folklore, said to haunt the ancient streets, churches, and catacombs of Kyiv, one of Eastern Europes oldest and most historically layered cities. This spectral figure is most commonly identified as the spirit of a murdered monk or soldier from centuries past, bound to the earthly realm by unfinished business or violent death. The ghost is intimately connected to Kyievs rich history, which spans over 1,500 years including the Kyivan Rus period, Mongol invasions, Cossack uprisings, and modern conflicts. Depending on the tale, the Kiev Ghost appears to those who are in need, offering cryptic warnings, guidance to hidden treasures, or reassurance during times of crisis. The ghost embodies Ukraines complex and often tragic history, serving as a spiritual guardian of the nations cultural heritage and ancestral memory
source: Ukrainian folklore; hauntings of Kyiv streets, documented in local urban legends.

name: Killer Whale
description: The Killer Whale, known as Sgaana in the Haida language, is a profoundly significant supernatural being in Haida mythology and the broader Indigenous folklore of the Pacific Northwest coast of Canada. These majestic creatures are not mere animals but are considered powerful spirit beings, the rulers of the ocean, and the ancestors of the Haida people transformed into their present form. In Haida tradition, Killer Whales live in immense underwater villages organized just like human communities, with houses, chiefs, and potlatch ceremonies conducted beneath the waves. They are believed to be the reincarnations of great Haida chiefs and warriors who chose to become protectors of the sea after death. The relationship between the Haida and the Killer Whale is one of deep mutual respect, with the whales serving as helpers, guides, and symbols of clan identity. They feature prominently in Haida art, with their forms carved into totem poles, house posts, and ceremonial objects
source: Haida spiritual tradition; documented in Northwest Coast records.

name: Kim Qui (Golden Turtle God)
description: Kim Qui (literally 'Golden Turtle') is the sacred turtle god of Vietnamese mythology who helped King An Dương Vương build the spiral-shaped Cổ Loa Citadel and forge a magic crossbow that could fire hundreds of arrows at once. According to legend, Kim Qui emerged from the waters and revealed to the king how to construct the citadel's defensive walls, which had kept collapsing until the turtle god explained they were built on a mountain spirit's territory. After appeasing the spirit, the walls stood firm. Kim Qui also gave the king one of his claws to use as a trigger for the magic crossbow, granting the kingdom invincibility. The turtle god later appeared when the foreign prince Trọng Thủy had replaced the claw with a fake, revealing the betrayal to the fleeing king. In the legend of Hoàn Kiếm Lake, the Golden Turtle emerged to reclaim the magical sword Thuận Thiên (Heaven's Will) from Emperor Lê Lợi, declaring that Heaven had lent the sword to expel the Ming invaders and now required its return. Kim Qui remains a powerful symbol of Vietnamese independence, sovereignty, and divine protection
source: Vietnamese folk religion — Kim Quy golden turtle god.

name: Kinnara (Celestial Musician)
description: Kinnaras are half-human, half-bird celestial beings from Hindu and Buddhist mythology, renowned as divine musicians and lovers. Described in the Mahabharata, they are eternal lovers who never separate, never bearing children but forever embracing. They come from the Himalayas and are known for their exquisite music, dance, and poetry. In Hindu iconography, they are depicted with a human torso and head atop a bird's lower body, or sometimes as half-horse, half-human centaur-like beings. The Vishnudharmottara describes them as half-man and half-horse, while Buddhist traditions portray them as half-man and half-bird. Kinnaras are gentle, harmless creatures who hop like birds, love music and song, with females beating drums and males playing lutes. Their food consists of flower pollen, their cosmetics are made from flower perfumes, and they dress in garlands. The female Kinnari is a traditional symbol of feminine beauty, grace, and accomplishment across South and Southeast Asia
source: Mahabharata (Adi Parva), Jataka tales, Vishnudharmottara Purana, Hindu and Buddhist mythology

name: Kitchi-Manitou
description: Kitchi-Manitou, also known as Gitche Manitou or Gichi-manidoo, is the Great Spirit in the spiritual traditions of Algonquian-speaking Native American peoples of the United States, including the Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Menominee, and other tribes of the Great Lakes region. As the supreme creative force in the universe, Kitchi-Manitou is understood as the source from which all life, energy, and spiritual power emanate. Unlike the personified gods of many other religious traditions, Kitchi-Manitou represents a more abstract, all-pervasive spiritual reality that connects every aspect of existence in a sacred web of relationships. This concept of the Great Spirit is central to the traditional worldview that governs how people relate to each other, to nature, and to the spiritual realm. Kitchi-Manitou is the ultimate authority behind the Midewiwin or Grand Medicine Society, the traditional spiritual organization that has preserved sacred knowledge across generations
source: Ojibwe/Algonquian religion — Kitchimanitou is the Great Spirit of Algonquian cosmology.

name: Kitsunebi
description: Kitsunebi, meaning "fox fire" in Japanese, are mysterious floating lights that appear in forests and rural areas of Japan, closely associated with the presence of kitsune fox spirits. These ethereal flames are believed to be a manifestation of the kitsune supernatural power, created when the spirits exhale or conjure fire as they move through the darkness. Witnesses describe the kitsunebi as small orbs of colored light that drift silently through the trees, sometimes appearing as a single light and other times as a long procession of flames stretching across the landscape. The phenomenon has been documented in Japanese folklore for centuries and is often cited as an explanation for the will-o-the-wisp or hitodama ghost lights seen in marshy or forested areas. Kitsunebi are deeply woven into the fabric of Japanese folk belief, representing the mysterious and often deceptive nature of the fox spirits that create them
source: Japanese folklore; Kitsunebi are fox-fires created by Kitsune.

name: Klabautermann
description: The Klabautermann is a water-kobold and ship spirit in Frisian, German, and Dutch maritime folklore — a small, pipe-smoking sailor-specter who resides aboard seagoing vessels from their very construction until their sinking. He is an ambiguous figure, simultaneously a guardian spirit who protects the crew and an omen of doom whose visible appearance foretells certain shipwreck. According to tradition, the Klabautermann enters a ship through its timber: if a stillborn or unbaptized child was buried under a tree later used for shipbuilding, its soul becomes the Klabautermann. By night he works small miracles — repairing broken tackle, pumping out leaks, coiling ropes, and polishing brass — so that sailors wake to a perfectly maintained ship. But if the crew becomes lazy, drunken, or blasphemous, he turns malicious, tangling rigging, hiding tools, and slapping sailors across the face with invisible hands. When the ship is doomed, he reveals himself, then abandons the vessel to its fate In Germany folklore, this figure is known among the Germany people.
source: German/Frisian maritime folklore; the Klabautermann is a ship spirit.

name: Kobold
description: The Kobold is one of the most versatile and widespread spirits in Germanic folklore, inhabiting homes, mines, ships, and natural spaces throughout Germany and surrounding regions. These small, impish beings belong to a broad category of household and nature spirits that can be either helpful or mischievous depending on how they are treated. The name kobold literally means "house dweller" and reflects their close association with human habitation. Kobolds are deeply rooted in Germanic folk belief, with different varieties inhabiting different environments: Hauskobolde (house kobolds), Bergkobolde (mine kobolds), and Schiffkobolde (ship kobolds). They are considered neither fully good nor fully evil but rather morally ambiguous beings whose behavior mirrors the treatment they receive. The English word "cobalt" derives from kobold, as medieval miners blamed the troublesome spirit for contaminating silver ore with unwanted cobalt
source: Germany mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Kodama
description: Kodama are ancient tree spirits from Japanese folklore, believed to inhabit the oldest and most magnificent trees in the forest. The name kodama literally means "tree spirit" or "echo," reflecting the belief that mysterious sounds heard in the mountains are the voices of these spirits. Kodama are deeply respected in Shinto tradition, where trees are considered living entities with souls deserving of reverence. The spirits are particularly associated with the cedar, camphor, and pine trees that grow in sacred groves around Shinto shrines. Cutting down a tree inhabited by a kodama is considered an act of terrible disrespect that brings curses, illness, and misfortune upon the perpetrator and their family. The belief in kodama reflects the Japanese animistic worldview that sees spiritual presence in all natural phenomena, encouraging environmental stewardship and respect for the living forest
source: Japanese mythology; Kodama are tree spirits that inhabit ancient forests.

name: Kola Sanni Yaka
description: Kola Sanni Yaka is a fearsome demon of disease and spirit possession from Sri Lankan folklore, belonging to the Sanni Yakka pantheon of eighteen demons collectively responsible for causing specific illnesses and afflictions. This particular yaka is associated with severe physical and mental ailments, with its name deriving from kola meaning leaf or herbal medicine and sanni meaning disease or affliction. The Sanni Yakka tradition is deeply embedded in the Sinhalese Buddhist healing practices, where these demons are not considered purely evil but rather as powerful beings that can cause harm when offended or improperly acknowledged. The rituals to appease these demons involve complex exorcisms called tovil, which combine dance, drumming, chanting, and offerings. Kola Sanni Yaka is particularly feared for its ability to cause debilitating conditions that resist conventional medical treatment, requiring the intervention of trained exorcists called edura
source: Sri lanka mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Kongamato
description: The Kongamato is a legendary flying creature from Zambian folklore, described as a large, bat-like monster that inhabits the swamps and rivers of the remote regions of Zambia, Angola, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The name kongamato means "overwhelmer of boats" in the Kaonde language, reflecting the creatures reputation for attacking and capsizing watercraft. This cryptid has captured the imagination of both local populations and Western explorers, with reported sightings dating from the colonial era through the present day. The Kongamato is often compared to the prehistoric pterosaur or pterodactyl by cryptozoologists who suggest it may be a surviving species of flying reptile. The creature is deeply feared by local communities who avoid its known habitats and report that it attacks without provocation, killing humans and large animals alike with devastating efficiency using its sharp beak and powerful claws
source: Zambian cryptozoology — the Kongamato flying cryptid from Zambian/Kaonde oral tradition.

name: Koreisha (Geongumi)
description: Koreisha, also known as Geongumi or Wonhon, is a type of vengeful ghost from Korean folklore, the spirit of a person who died with a deep grudge or under unjust circumstances. These restless souls are unable to move on to the afterlife because of the powerful negative emotions that bind them to the earthly realm. Koreisha are most commonly the spirits of women who died tragically, often due to social injustice, betrayal, or violence, reflecting the historical struggles of women in Korean society. The belief in koreisha is deeply rooted in Korean shamanism, where death is not seen as an end but as a transition that can be disrupted by unresolved emotions. These ghosts serve as powerful reminders of the importance of justice, proper funeral rites, and addressing social wrongs. The Korean concept of han, a feeling of unresolved resentment, is central to understanding the koreisha condition
source: Korean folklore; vengeful ghosts (Koreisha) who haunt locations until resolved.

name: Korkyt
description: Korkyt is the legendary founding father of Kazakh music, a revered sage, composer, poet, and philosopher who is credited with creating the kobyz, an ancient Kazakh stringed instrument, as well as the dombra, the national instrument of Kazakhstan. According to tradition, Korkyt lived for three hundred years, traveling the world to escape death and sharing his wisdom with all who would listen. He is considered the first baksy or shaman-musician, whose kobyz playing had the power to heal the sick, drive away evil spirits, and communicate with the spirit world. Korkyt occupies a unique position in Kazakh folklore as both a historical figure and a mythological hero whose legend has shaped the musical and spiritual traditions of the Kazakh people for centuries. His stories and compositions continue to be central to Kazakh cultural identity
source: Kazakh folklore — Korkyt Ata legendary bard and shaman.

name: Kosenjōbi
description: Kosenj is a type of tsukumogami from Japanese folklore, a spirit that inhabits old lamps and lanterns that have been used for a hundred years or more. The name kosenj literally means "old thousand-day fire" and refers to the belief that objects of illumination, particularly andon paper lamps and chochin lanterns, develop their own consciousness and spirit after a century of faithful service. These yokai are part of the broader tsukumogami tradition in Japanese folklore, where everyday objects that reach their centennial anniversary become animated by spirits. Kosenj are typically associated with the warm season when they are most active, floating through summer nights with their flames flickering eerily. Like many tsukumogami, kosenj are neither purely good nor evil but reflect the treatment they received during their years of service, becoming playful or malicious depending on how they were cared for
source: Japanese folklore; tsukumogami spirits of old lanterns.

name: Koyemsi
description: Koyemsi, also known as the Mudhead or Kachina Clown, is a distinctive figure in Hopi and Puebloan spiritual traditions of the Southwestern United States. These sacred clowns play a vital role in Hopi kachina ceremonies, serving as both entertainers and spiritual teachers who use humor and mockery to reinforce proper social behavior. Unlike the solemn kachinas that represent deities and ancestors, Koyemsi figures are deliberately comical and sometimes crude, using slapstick, mimicry, and parody to convey important cultural lessons. They are considered powerful spiritual beings despite their ridiculous appearance, capable of wielding profound spiritual force precisely because they operate outside normal social constraints. The Koyemsi tradition reflects the Hopi understanding that laughter and humility are essential components of spiritual life, and that the most profound truths can sometimes be conveyed through comedy
source: Hopi spiritual tradition; documented in Southwestern ethnographic records.

name: Kräkl (or Kratt)
description: Krakl, also spelled Kratt or Kraat, is a artificial being from Estonian folklore, a construct created by sorcerers from natural and household materials and animated through dark magic. Like the more common kratt, the krakl is a servitor created to perform tasks for its master, ranging from everyday chores to supernatural theft. However, the krakl is distinguished by its more rudimentary construction and more dangerous temperament, being considered a cruder and less reliable version of the kratt. The belief in such artificial beings is deeply rooted in Estonian and broader Finno-Ugric folk tradition, where the boundary between the natural and supernatural was fluid, and where clever but morally compromised individuals sought to gain advantage through spiritual deals. The krakl legend reflects the cultural understanding that shortcuts to prosperity come with hidden costs
source: Estonian folklore; variation of the kratt, often described as cruder versions.

name: Krahang
description: Krahang is a malevolent nocturnal spirit from Laotian and Thai folklore, a cursed ghost that takes the form of a shirtless man who flies through the night sky using traditional rice winnowing baskets as makeshift wings. This terrifying apparition is said to be the result of a curse placed upon a man who practiced forbidden dark arts or committed terrible sins during his lifetime, condemning him to wander the night as a tormented spirit. Krahang is considered the male counterpart to the more famous Krasue ghost, and the two are sometimes said to travel together. By day, the Krahang appears as an ordinary villager, indistinguishable from anyone else, but when night falls, the curse transforms him into a flying horror that preys on the living. The belief in Krahang is deeply embedded in rural Laotian culture, where reports of strange flying figures and mysterious nocturnal activities are often attributed to this spirit
source: Laos mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Krahom
description: Krahom is a vengeful ghost from Cambodian folklore, the restless spirit of a person who died a violent or unjust death, bound to the earthly realm by the intensity of their final emotions. The name krahom reflects the deep connection between violent death and spiritual unrest in Khmer tradition, where improper death creates lingering spirits that cannot find peace. These ghosts are particularly feared in rural Cambodia, where they are blamed for a wide range of misfortunes from illness and crop failure to accidents and unexplained deaths. The Krahom is not inherently malicious but becomes dangerous because its suffering and anger twist its nature. The belief in such spirits reflects the importance of proper funeral rites and the resolution of grievances in Khmer Buddhist culture, where the living have a responsibility to help the dead move on to their next existence through merit-making ceremonies and compassionate action
source: Cambodia mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Kraken
description: The Kraken is a legendary colossal sea monster said to dwell off the coasts of Norway and Greenland. Described as a giant octopus or squid-like creature, the Kraken was feared by Norwegian fishermen for its ability to drag entire ships and crews to the ocean depths. First described in detail by Norwegian Bishop Erik Pontoppidan in his work The Natural History of Norway (1753), who portrayed the Kraken as an enormous floating island-like creature with massive tentacles. When the Kraken submerged, it created a powerful whirlpool (mahlstrøm). The creature was said to be so large that fishermen sometimes mistook it for an island and landed on its back. The Kraken's name comes from the Norwegian word krake meaning unhealthy or twisted animal. Now one of the world's most famous legendary sea monsters, appearing in literature from Alfred Lord Tennyson to Pirates of the Caribbean
source: Scandinavian folklore; the Kraken is a colossal sea monster of the North Atlantic.

name: Krsnik
description: Krsnik is a vampire hunter from Slovenian and Croatian folklore, a special individual born with supernatural abilities that enable them to see, track, and destroy vampires and other undead creatures. The name krsnik derives from krs meaning cross or baptism, reflecting the Christian folk beliefs mixed with older pagan traditions that characterize these warriors. Krsniks are believed to be born with a caul or born on a Saturday, signs that mark them as chosen for this sacred duty. They operate at the boundary between the human world and the supernatural, possessing spiritual vision that allows them to see vampires in their true forms even when they appear as ordinary people. The krsnik tradition represents a unique blend of Christian and pre-Christian Slavic beliefs about the undead, combining Church-sanctioned methods such as holy water and crosses with older folk magic
source: Slovenian folklore; vampire hunters born with supernatural abilities.

name: Kulfre
description: Kulfre is a mountain spirit from Albanian folklore, a mysterious phantom that haunts the peaks and ridges of the Albanian Alps. This supernatural being is most commonly described as a headless humanoid figure that dances on mountaintops, appearing at night as a luminous ball of fire or a glowing human shape that moves with an eerie, fluid grace. The kulfre is deeply connected to the ancient Illyrian and Balkan beliefs that mountains are sacred spaces where the boundary between the human world and the spirit realm is thin. Unlike the more dangerous spirits of Albanian tradition, the kulfre is not actively malevolent but rather a neutral supernatural phenomenon, a remnant of older pagan beliefs that persisted alongside Christianity. Its appearances are considered omens, though whether for good or ill depends on the tradition and the circumstances of the encounter
source: Albanian folklore — spirit documented in Albanian oral tradition.

name: Kulshedra
description: Kulshedra is a colossal multi-headed female dragon from Albanian folklore, one of the most feared and powerful creatures in Balkan mythology. This monstrous serpentine being is associated with water, storms, and fire, commanding the primal forces of nature and bringing either drought or flood to the land depending on her mood. Kulshedra is the ancient enemy of the drangue, a heroic winged warrior who protects humanity from her depredations. The legend of kulshedra represents the eternal cosmic struggle between order and chaos, with the dragon embodying the untamed, destructive aspects of nature that must be constantly opposed by heroic forces. Her lairs are said to be deep caves near water sources, where she hoards treasure and the bones of her victims. The kulshedra legend is deeply rooted in the pre-Christian Illyrian and Balkan mythological traditions that persisted through centuries of cultural change
source: Albanian folklore — Kulshedra is a dragon documented in Albanian oral tradition.

name: Kuman Thong
description: Kuman Thong is a household spirit from Thai folklore, the animated spirit of a child that has been bound to a golden statue through black magic rituals. The name Kuman Thong means "Golden Child Spirit," and these beings are created through complex and controversial ceremonies performed by traditional sorcerers known as wei monks or ajahn. Originally, the creation of a Kuman Thong involved the remains of a child who died in the womb or shortly after birth, but modern practice typically uses consecrated statues. These spirits are believed to bring good luck, protection, and wealth to their owners if properly cared for, but they can become dangerous if neglected or mistreated. The belief in Kuman Thong reflects the Thai spiritual tradition of animistic household spirits combined with Buddhist and Brahmanic elements, where the spirit world is intimately connected with daily life
source: Thailand mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections
